Demand for climate change adaptation has continued to grow, creating new opportunities across regions.

WWF FINLAND 2025

Uptake of climate adaptation measures has steadily increased throughout the programme’s implementation, among both communities and authorities. In 2024, a total of 33 adaptation plans and NbS initiatives received support under the programme. Demand for climate change adaptation has continued to grow, creating new opportunities across regions. Africa Adaptation Hub, together with WWF offices and partners, played a key role in advancing adaptation interventions, capacitybuilding, and regional advocacy. Meanwhile in Bolivia, significant efforts were made to strengthen the capacity of municipalities in climate adaptation and fire management, with successful

approaches already being replicated elsewhere. These developments have contributed to surpassing the targets set for this programme output. Implementation of NbS and adaptation interventions goes hand in hand with capacity building and skills development. Throughout 2024, the programme supported both rights holders and duty bearers in enhancing the adaptive capacities of communities, CSOs, and government counterparts. Through the Papua programme, WWF Indonesia assisted the Sundoy clan in drafting a management plan aimed at conserving forest and marine ecosystems within their ancestral lands. The area under traditional stewardship covers 9,921.87 hectares. A training on NbS for adaptation for WWF staff and CSO partners from Kenya, Uganda, Madagascar, Tanzania, and Somalia was convened as a joint effort by Africa Adaptation Hub and Voices for Just Climate Action (VCA) Alliance in Kenya. Also, CSOs and Pan-African youth networks (from Kavango-Zambezi, Greater Virunga Landscape and Southwestern Indian Ocean landscapes, as well as Kenya and Mozambique) were capacitated by Africa Adaptation Hub to enhance their influence on climate adaptation and natural resource governance and equipping them to integrate climate resilience strategies into their work. In Madagascar, CSO representatives and regional decision-makers received training on climate change challenges and policy strategies in order to strengthen their role in regional adaptation planning and advocacy. Similarly in Nepal, municipality authorities from seven municipalities were trained on climate change, disaster risk reduction and environment-friendly planning and the programme contributed to a partnership and project development between the International Federations of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) and WWF Nepal. A series of training activities and workshops were held in Bolivia to capacitate both local civil society representatives, such as cocoa producers, livestock farmers, indigenous peoples’ representatives, people with disability and government authorities and technicians in forest fire prevention and management, as well as emergency response and inclusive management. Thanks to the skills and support provided by the programme, trained participants in one municipality were able to control a wildfire and protect nearby homes from

Programme has supported firefighting efforts in Bolivia for many years, in 2024 also with additional funding from WWF Finland’s Natural Disaster Fund. © MPINTO / WWF-BOLIVIA

destruction. During the devastating 2024 wildfire season in Bolivia, WWF Finland allocated additional resources from its Natural Disaster Fund to WWF Bolivia. This funding supported on-the-ground firefighting efforts, including the provision of essential equipment, medical supplies, and logistical aid to affected municipalities. Climate related decision-making processes influenced and climate financing leveraged through advocacy

The Africa Adaptation Hub also contributed to WWF’s position for climate COP negotiations.

WWF FINLAND 2025

In 2024, a total of 12 climate-related decisionmaking processes were influenced through programme efforts. At the regional level in Africa, climate advocacy was advanced through the Adaptation Hub, which operates as a key partner of the African Wildlife Foundation (AWF) in promoting climate adaptation and the role of protected areas. One major engagement was the Hub’s participation in the African Protected Area Directors (APAD) Conference, which brought together over 150 stakeholders including protected area directors, government officials, youth representatives, civil society organisations, private

sector actors, donors, NGOs, and representatives of Indigenous Peoples and local communities. As a result of this engagement, a five-year MoU was signed between APAD and AWF. The memorandum aims to enhance the contribution of Africa’s protected and conservation areas to global biodiversity and climate goals. With support from the programme, the Adaptation Hub will provide technical assistance for implementing the climate adaptation component of this agreement. The Africa Adaptation Hub also contributed to WWF’s position for climate COP negotiations by coauthoring the WWF Africa Expectations Paper for COP29. This document was widely disseminated across multiple platforms and formally presented to the African Group of Negotiators (AGN), helping to amplify WWF’s message, align with AGN priorities, and influence the COP29 negotiation outcomes. In addition, the Hub organised four side events at COP29, focusing on key themes including adaptation finance, NbS, climate–biodiversity

integration, and innovative financing mechanisms for Protected and Conserved Areas (PCAs). The Hub also developed and launched a policy brief together with the WWF network on “Enhancing Adaptation in NDC: Analysis and Reflections from 19 African countries” to inform on the development of a strong adaptation component in the next round of nationally determined contributions (NDC 3.0) for 2025. The analysis highlights that while many countries acknowledge climate risks, gaps remain in locally led adaptation, monitoring and evaluation and alignment with national adaptation plans (NAP), and emphasizes the need for increased adaptation finance, clear financial indicators, and stronger safeguards against maladaptive practices, in order to enhance resilience and long-term sustainability. Original assumptions of the Results Framework are still valid:
• Stakeholders support climate mitigation and adaptation actions
• Conducive environment for CSOs to influence policies/ plans and strategies exists

At programme level, cooperation was carried out with 11 women’s rights and gender equality CSOs, 13 disability-focused CSOs, and 10 indigenous peoples’ organisations.

The Africa Adaptation Hub has far exceeded its target for engaging CSO partners. Against an initial target of 10, the Hub has reached 81 CSOs to date. This overachievement was made possible by delivering capacity-building support across major regional landscape programmes, including the Kavango-Zambezi Transfrontier Conservation Area (KAZA), the Greater Virunga Landscape (GVL), and the South West Indian Ocean region. These workshops equipped CSO representatives from Pan-African Youth network (Young Volunteers for the Environment), women-led organizations (such as Akina Mama wa Afrika in Kenya and Katara Women in GVL), marine conservation organisations, rural development organisations and humanitarian NGOs, with the knowledge and skills needed to drive impactful NbS adaptation interventions and climate resilience efforts in their communities. There were no significant changes on the status of the civic space in the partner countries in 2024. Globally the situation for environmental human rights defenders remains challenging. partners even in the countries where civic space might be limited, by bringing additional technical support for the line ministries and agencies. WWF helps also to communicate government decisions and regulations to the local communities and districts, for example in Indonesia. WWF FINLAND 2025

Other programme partners have also exceeded expectations in their policy engagement, responding to unanticipated opportunities or increased demand for WWF’s input, that arose after the initial targets were set. The programme supported the participation of WWF staff to University of Eastern Finland (UEF) training on Multilateral Environmental Agreements, organized together with UNEP. As geopolitical dynamics increasingly shape environmental negotiations, it is essential to equip NGOs with the skills needed for strategic, informed, and impactful participation. WWF supported three staff members from Uganda, Madagascar, and Indonesia to participate in the two-week long training, and all participants found the course highly beneficial for their work. Later, one participant took part in the COP29 and COP16 meetings. WWF Finland continued its efforts to reduce the negative impacts of production and consumption on biodiversity and climate by promoting awareness and action on ecological footprints. At the international level, WWF Finland supported the WWF network on this theme – most notably by organising a side event at COP16 titled “Momentum for Target 16: Enhancing Collective Action to Reduce the Global Footprint of Consumption Equitably.” In this side-event WWF brought together key players to support the idea of tackling overconsumption in order to enable achieving the Global Biodiversity Framework. WWF Finland invited the Finnish cooperative conglomerate S-Group to participate in the side-event to present their experiences on mapping biodiversity impacts of their business. In COP16 WWF Finland also supported Finland to join the new Champions group on mainstreaming. This group brings together countries which recognise the urgent need to halt and reverse biodiversity loss across sectors. Like many other Finnish NGOs, WWF Finland is deeply concerned about the significant budget cuts made by the current government to Finland’s development cooperation funding. Unfortunately, this is a worrying global trend. WWF Finland considers these cuts a threat to Finland’s credibility in global diplomacy, as they jeopardise the country’s ability to meet its international climate finance commitments and highlight the lack of progress in increasing biodiversity funding. Finland has been, and has considered itself, even in the present government paper, as a reliable and ambitious global entity which fulfills its international commitments. WWF Finland considers that Finland has fallen

short in meeting its international responsibilities, particularly evident during the 2024 COP negotiations on both climate and biodiversity. This concern was also communicated to the Finnish media. Public officials and other duty bearers capacitated and supported in natural resources governance and climate adaptation

Working with government actors (duty bearers) and providing them with technical support is a key role that WWF plays across all partner countries.

In 2024, through this programme, WWF provided capacity-building and support to several duty bearers in all partner countries, including Finland. However, only 42% of the overall target has been achieved at this stage of the programme, which is lower than expected. Of those reached so far, 31% were women. That said, in several countries the programme has exceeded expectations. In Bolivia, for example, 60 public officials have received training, far surpassing the original target of six. This overachievement is largely due to a successful consultation process that involved more government representatives than initially planned, particularly in relation to the Ramsar site management plan.

The largest deviation from the overall target stems from the East Africa Wildlife Crime Hub (EAWCH), as it is targeting to capacitate 10,000 duty bearers during the programme, a figure significantly higher than those set by other partners. This difference is explained by the fact that the Hub primarily trains rangers, rather than public officials from local government offices or partner country ministries, as is the case for other implementing partners. OUTPUT 3.1 WWF TOGETHER WITH DUTY BEARERS AND RIGHTS HOLDERS HAS CO-CREATED SOLUTIONS TO TACKLE ILLEGAL WILDLIFE AND TIMBER TRADE, POACHING AND HUMAN WILDLIFE CONFLICTS Trend (number, frequency and intensity) in levels of Human Wildlife Conflict (HWC) incidents Partners reporting to this indicator are Borneo, Nepal, Uganda and EAWCH, with the indicator a declining trend – specific numeric target has

WWF FINLAND 2025

not been set. Around the world, Human Wildlife Conflict (HWC) challenges people and wildlife, leading to a decrease in people’s tolerance for conservation efforts and contributing to multiple factors that drive species to extinction. WWF supported the development of the Conflict to Coexistence (C2C) approach in collaboration with subject-matter experts and partner organisations. C2C is an integrated, stepwise approach to enable systematic HWC management planning, implementation, and monitoring. The East Africa Wildlife Crime Hub (EAWCH) played a key role in shaping the C2C approach, offering technical input during its development. The Hub further supported its localisation in the Ruvuma Landscape and is now facilitating its implementation in the Greater Virunga Landscape, with initial focus on Queen Elizabeth National Park. During dry periods, wildlife often enters human settlements in search of water and food, increasing the risk of conflict. In East Africa, higher-than-average rainfall in 2024 has led to a slight overall decrease in such incidents. However, regional conflicts involving hyenas are on the rise, and elephant-related conflicts remain consistently high across the region.

Human-wildlife conflict management has become more critical than ever.

In Nepal, the frequency of HWC remains high. There’s been a significant increase in wildlife populations, for example the tiger population nearly tripling over the past decade, whilst the Terai Arc Landscape is densely populated by humans. As a result, human-wildlife conflict management has become more critical than ever. Many species use the forest areas within corridors as their extended habitats and there is frequent movement of wildlife from forests to agricultural lands. To address these challenges, the programme provided support (with additional EUR 25,000 from unallocated funding) for various interventions aimed at minimising negative human-wildlife interactions and mitigating their impacts on communities through preventive and remedial measures. Preventive measures include early warning systems, fencing, alternative livelihood options, and training on wildlife behaviour, rescue and HWC sensitisation, whereas remedial measures include relief funds and insurance schemes. The programme supported the installation of 554 meters of mesh wire fencing, 1,450 meters of electric fencing, 17 sirens and 35 LPGs in corridors and buffer zones, benefiting 2,517 HHs (1,140 IPs) as preventive measures of HWC. The escalation of HWC in Nepal has led to increasing insecurity among local communities, reducing tolerance for wildlife and fueling frustration toward conservation efforts. In some areas, albeit not in programme implementing sites, retaliatory killings of tigers have surged further complicating conservation initiatives. Simultaneously, the growing number of injuries and fatalities from wildlife attacks have intensified demands for immediate relief, compensation and mitigation measures. Insufficient knowledge of animal behaviour and a lack of adaptive human responses continue to be key factors driving the escalation of conflict. Demonstrable progress in implementation of the Zero Poaching Framework

The Greater Virunga Landscape has achieved zero poaching of mountain gorillas since 2022.

WWF FINLAND 2025

EAWCH is the only partner contributing to the target. However, related efforts have also been supported in Borneo to reduce poaching activity. The programme aims to achieve poaching reductions in three key landscapes in Eastern Africa: the Greater Virunga Landscape, Laikipia, and SOKNOT. To date, two of these landscapes have reported zero poaching of target species. The Greater Virunga Landscape has achieved zero poaching of mountain gorillas since 2022. The EAWCH supported the development and implementation of the regional zero poaching

strategy supporting all the gorilla parks. The adoption of a zero poaching strategy for rhinos by the Kenya Wildlife Service has been instrumental in achieving zero poaching incidents in multiple landscapes, including Laikipia. In both GVL and Laikipia there’s been improvement in capacity and the use of technology. In the Mara region of SOKNOT, no cases of rhino or elephant poaching have been reported. While elephant poaching across East Africa is generally low, only a few protected areas have reached the benchmark of zero poaching. In Borneo, WWF continued its collaboration with the West Kalimantan SMART Forum to support the implementation of SMART monitoring by forest management units across the province. Beyond aligning programme approaches with government plans, mobilising additional funding plays a critical role in ensuring the sustainability of programme achievements, particularly in light of the global decline in official development assistance (ODA). Africa programme, where WWF will partner with the Kenya Wildlife Conservancies Association, Rhino Ark and ICRAF. On a smaller scale, in Uganda, cooperatives and community groups that have been strengthened with support from the programme have shown increasing ability to attract small-scale funding from a variety of sources. Several cooperatives reported success in obtaining small grants, support from local government programmes and other development partners. Partnerships and coalitions developed

Most partners have carried on a level of cooperation with local disability organisations, gender-focused organisations and indigenous people organisations.

The programme has developed more than twice the number of partnerships and coalitions originally targeted. In addition to the old partnerships, all programme partners along with WWF Finland have been able to create new partnerships, which verifies that WWF is still seen as a relevant partner in all programme countries including Finland. After the new Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework the interest in addressing biodiversity loss has increased, which has strengthened WWF’s role in establishing partnerships and coalitions. In Finland, 2024 saw the launch of more formal collaboration with the Finnish Institute of International Affairs (FIIA) and the University of Eastern Finland. Through this cooperation, several WWF partners received capacity-building support. Free, Prior and Informed consent (FPIC) consultations held and Environmental and Social Safeguards (ESSF) processes supported

WWF implements free, prior and informed consent procedures and principles when working with communities and especially indigenous peoples. The programme has significantly exceeded its target for ESSF and FPIC processes, achieving 271% of the planned total for the programme period. This is because all partners have applied safeguards procedures in their projects and / or landscapes and the use of FPIC has become an integral part of working together with the communities in any activity. In the programme implementation, FPIC is not only done once but repeated in cases where collaboration in a new approach or activity is started. In addition to WWF guidance, some offices like Nepal have developed their own context specific and formalised guidelines to facilitate conducting FPIC together with national IP organisations. To ensure safeguards are properly addressed, a functioning grievance mechanism is essential. All programme countries now have such mechanisms in place. Community awareness of these systems has been strengthened through training, awarenessraising activities, the installation of additional grievance boxes and the formation of grievance management sub-committees. It’s important to note that the program promotes and creates local governance spaces for indigenous and local communities for decision making and management of their own territories and natural resources. Original assumptions of the Results Framework are still valid:
• Suitable legal instruments (policies and guidelines) are in place for sustainable financing mechanism
• Strategic partnerships identified, value added and vision shared among partners
• Indigenous peoples and local communities are willing to co-operate, WWF and its partners have adequate capacity

The programme has continued to adhere to the WWF network standards on environmental and social safeguards. Mitigation plans and environmental and social management frameworks have been developed and implemented according to the standards.

WWF FINLAND 2025

SUCCESSES, CHALLENGES AND LESSONS LEARNED

Villagers in West Papua. © TIITU SAARIKOSKI / WWF

WWF FINLAND 2025

In the third year of programme implementation, WWF Finland conducted a light reflection on its strengths and weaknesses as part of annual reporting. This included comparisons with other Finnish NGOs implementing similar support programmes, as well as with other WWF offices working with the same partner countries. The reflection was inspired by the mid-term review of the programme, meeting with the partners in Finland, development of the new programme, WWF Finland’s strategy revision and discussions with the stakeholders and WWF colleagues.

•

These reflections were as follows:

The programme’s close cooperation with local government forms a key foundation for the sustainability of its interventions.

WWF FINLAND 2025

• WWF Finland’s programme benefits from and contributes to the wider WWF network, which offers established systems and structures that support effective programme delivery. These include the whistleblowing mechanism, FPIC protocols, and grievance structures. By drawing on these existing tools, WWF Finland avoids duplicating efforts, ensures professional standards, and promotes transparency and accountability in a cost-effective manner.
• By comparison with some larger WWF “donor” offices, WWF Finland and its programme remain relatively small in scale. In certain partner countries, Finnish support may represent only a modest share of overall country-level funding. However, it continues to provide critical resources at the landscape level. As a result, WWF Finland may not always be perceived as a key actor in national-level dialogues within the network, despite its strategic contributions on the ground.
• The long-standing and respected presence of partner WWF offices plays a key role in ensuring the sustainability of programme approaches and strengthening civil society engagement at the national level. WWF’s reputation as a reliable and well-established actor provides a strong foundation for WWF Finland’s support. Joint planning with partner offices is also streamlined by the fact that all WWF network offices operate under a shared strategic framework. This framework, revised in 2024–25 as Roadmap 2030, reinforces the network’s collective contribution to global environmental commitments.
• WWF offices are widely recognised as strong and influential organisations within their respective countries. However, this prominent role as an international NGO (INGO) can sometimes be perceived as intimidating by smaller, local civil society organisations. To address this, the programme actively encourages its partners to engage and collaborate with local CSOs. WWF Finland also requires its partners to

•

•

•

•

report annually on their role within the broader civil society landscape. Being a big and strong organization might prevent WWF from being a quick and agile institution to react to possible changes. This is yet to create any challenges for WWF or the programme to operate, but we may need to learn from humanitarian organisations, e.g. how their programme management allows for quick changes. One of the key advantages of Finnish support within the WWF network has been its flexibility, allowing programme partners to adapt and make changes as needed. The option to utilise unallocated funds has been particularly valuable in enhancing this adaptability. To date, the changes made within the programme have remained relatively modest. The programme’s close cooperation with local government forms a key foundation for the sustainability of its interventions. WWF partners receive resources to support activities that are jointly planned with government actors, aligning both with national and local level development plans and WWF strategies. This model of collaboration resembles that of traditional bilateral development cooperation, where donor countries supported government capacitybuilding in specific sectors. However, unlike bilateral programmes — which often operate within limited timeframes — WWF’s long-term presence in partner countries allows for more sustained engagement. The programme’s support focuses primarily on strengthening government capacity at the community and district levels, rather than at the central ministry level, making it highly relevant and responsive to local needs. The programme funding has enabled WWF Finland to provide long-term support to its partners — a critical factor given WWF’s sustained engagement with local governments and civil society organisations. In the environmental sector especially, change tends to occur gradually, requiring long-term interventions to achieve lasting impact. Finland and its support might is seen as a neutral regarding international politics which can be seen as a good thing by the authoritites and government partners in the programme countries and help the local WWF to have smooth cooperation and coordinated work with authorities. The programme’s wide scope from communitylevel interventions and sub-national planning to national advocacy and participation in UN processes gives WWF and its partners a significant strategic advantage. Its on-the-ground presence, including work with indigenous peoples and local communities, provides vital insight into local realities. This knowledge can then be brought

WWF’s status as a well-recognised and respected organisation helps ensure that these communitygrounded perspectives are heard in international forums.

There are still challenges in promoting full participation of women in the programme activities.

into policy discussions in collaboration with smaller civil society organisations. WWF’s status as a well-recognised and respected organisation helps ensure that these community-grounded perspectives are heard in international forums, including the UN. The credibility of WWF and its partners in the eyes of international institutions stems not only from their global reach, but from their tangible connection to grassroots conservation and climate action.
• Over the years under the programme support from MFA, WWF Finland has strengthened its role and work in Finland. Establishing its role among the other development organisations with strong and reliable expertise on environment and climate change has been enabled with the programme funding. WWF’s ability to reflect its experiences from the developing country partners’ work to the international agreements connected to the Finnish policy processes and Sustainable Development Goals national dialogue has been widely appreciated.
• Building global equity issues to WWF’s communication has also developed over the years. WWF Finland has a vast number of followers in social media where it reaches audiences which might not be reached by other, more development cooperation focused organisations. Also, WWF’s visibility on international topics has increased remarkably in traditional media during the past few years. WWF Finland’s views are frequently cited, especially related to the UN processes on biodiversity and climate. In 2024, there was public dialogue on localisation and balances of power relating to development cooperation. The balance of power in partnerships between international organisations like WWF, even when operating as locally established NGOs, and local CSO and CBO partners requires greater recognition. While efforts toward localisation and the empowerment of local organisations are underway, further progress is still needed. Large organisations are sometimes perceived as transactional or consultative in their approach, rather than truly empowering; particularly when they control access to financial resources. Strengthening equitable partnerships and shifting more ownership to local actors remains a critical area for development. Although the activities are planned and implemented together, the possible dependency on funding from another organisation may already create a power imbalance between partners if no adequate measures are taken. Ways to balance these power relations need to be further identified. Some of the so far identified ways to create more equal partnerships

WWF FINLAND 2025

and locally led conservation include allowing more flexible implementation and budgeting, in addition to supporting local coalition building. Having an opportunity to provide financial support directly to the local CSOs and have them to prioritise the use of funds is found to be challenging due to donor requirements. Sometimes strategically most relevant CSO partners, especially in remote areas, do not fulfil, for instance, the financial management criteria of the donors. Therefore, the local WWF office is left with the options of either jeopardising the conservation results or absorbing the risk themselves. There are still challenges in promoting full participation of women in the programme activities. In many programme villages, a strong patriarchal hierarchy remains, where women have traditionally not had the right to hold positions such as group leaders or primary household income earners. Women are also often very busy with the many responsibilities assigned to them. A key challenge observed during monitoring trips is the limited visibility and participation of women, as meetings are often male-dominated. This is reflected at the programme level, where the proportion of female beneficiaries is lower than that of males. For instance, the number of small businesses operated by women remains comparatively low. Furthermore, the number of female smallholder farmers within the programme is lower than that of men. The programme aims to address these issues and further improve the status of women in its implementation. Efforts to improve disability inclusion continue. During the programme partner visit to Finland in autumn, a disability inclusion refresher training was held in cooperation with the Abilis Foundation. During 2024, partners conducted disability inclusion trainings for stakeholders, including government officials and local communities in countries like Tanzania, Laos, and Bolivia, and carried out needs assessments in remote communities – such as in Papua and Bolivia – leading to improved services and emergency preparedness for persons with disabilities, for instance during forest fire crises. There are also challenges in promoting disability inclusion. It remains difficult to obtain comprehensive information on the number of rights holders with disabilities within the program. Persons with disabilities are only recorded as beneficiaries when they are individually identified through programme activities. In cases where entire villages are counted collectively, disability-specific data is typically not captured, often resulting in reported totals of zero,

Of the programme partners, Nepal has been a front-runner in disability inclusion. Sunita Danguara is one of those disabled people WWF has supported. She now runs her own food shop. © MUNA THAPA

The pace of inclusion for persons with disabilities remains limited and requires further attention.

even if this is unlikely to be accurate. Overall, the pace of inclusion for persons with disabilities remains limited and requires further attention. This may be due to WWF staff’s own lack of capacity on the matter but also due to existing hesitant attitudes in the programme villages towards people with disabilities. Another challenge is transportation needs in remote areas which also increase risks if for instance boat transportation is needed. The programme continues to build the capacity of staff and partners in disability inclusion through training and awareness raising. WWF Finland received support from a WWF International Innovation Team to facilitate dialogue from the mid-term review results towards the continued partnership 2026 onwards. The innovation team used an approach called 3 horizons to encourage WWF Finland and its partners to reflect the situation and look towards the future to inspire new possible approaches in order to reach the joint target. The external facilitation proved highly valuable, providing a structured framework for dialogue between WWF Finland and its partners. It also helped define concrete tasks for the partners to implement in collaboration with their local colleagues. The further use of this network resource will be explored in 2025. This also facilitates stronger integration of WWF Finland’s programme and approaches within the broader WWF network.

WWF FINLAND 2025

At the end of 2023 WWF Finland put out a tender for the mid-term evaluation of the programme. The time to submit the proposals was almost 4 weeks (20.12.2023 - 15.1.2024), but over the Christmas season the timing was probably not optimal. Also the budget, EUR 50,000, may have been considered too small by some possible evaluators. Despite this, WWF received two good proposals. Programme-level evaluations often present challenges in generating detailed observations and recommendations specific to individual countries. Some of the partners were expecting more detailed country level analysis, considering the time and resources they put on supporting the evaluators during their visits in the countries. Looking ahead, the budget allocated for programme-level evaluations should be increased to ensure more comprehensive analysis. In addition, the purpose and scope of these evaluations must be communicated more clearly to programme partners. Lessons were also gathered regarding the long-format monitoring trip approach. Longer monitoring visits offer valuable opportunities to explore specific topics in greater depth, particularly when there is a need to conceptualise new approaches — as seen in Papua, for example, in work on inclusive conservation and nature-based solutions for adaptation. These visits also enhance regular monitoring by allowing for a more nuanced understanding of complex issues.

When strategically planned, extended visits can also serve to coordinate efforts and generate synergies across WWF network offices and donors, aligning support and projects more effectively. However, it is important to recognise the potential for unintended power imbalances when proposing visits or joint processes between WWF Finland and partner offices. Such visits may lead partner offices to commit significant time and resources, even when this level of effort may not be necessary for the intended purpose. These dynamics should be discussed openly and transparently during the planning phase to ensure mutual clarity and avoid undue pressure.

Partnering countries and the WWF network provide WWF Finland with various communication materials.

WWF FINLAND 2025

In 2024, WWF Finland and its partners encountered significant challenges in securing visas for visits to Finland. In 2024, there were exceptionally many visits to Finland due to the cooperation with the University of Eastern Finland and the Partnership week in September. The partners were advised to apply for visas early on and all the required documentation was provided to them. Nevertheless, several colleagues faced challenges to obtain visas and one colleague didn’t manage to get one at all. The processing times for visas were long and colleagues needed to travel in order to submit the applications. Sometimes embassies asked for verification from WWF Finland but the request was sent to the wrong email addresses, which in turn caused delays on responses especially during the summer holidays. The whole visa process took a lot of time and effort both from WWF Finland as well as partner offices and it was disappointing that one key colleague was not issued a visa to participate in the joint meeting in Finland. It is understandable that Schengen visa process is tight but it’s unfortunate that the process is hindering the effective coordination of a Finnish funded programme, and despite being invited by WWF Finland to attend the programme workshop as one of the key persons in the programme, programme coordinator from a partner country is not issued a visa. Throughout 2024, WWF Finland maintained a strong focus on domestic advocacy while also supporting its partners’ advocacy initiatives, as previously described. In response to what WWF Finland viewed as Finland’s failure to uphold its international commitments at the 2024 COP meetings, both on climate and biodiversity, the organisation adopted a more outspoken and critical stance in public communications during autumn 2024. In the COP, COP, COP media event, which provided a briefing to the Finnish media on the three COP meetings; climate, biodiversity and desertification, WWF Finland clearly expressed its

concerns. Ahead of COP16, WWF Finland publicly criticised Finland’s lack of preparedness, stating that both the country and Minister Mykkänen were attending the meeting “empty-handed.” At the time, Finland’s national biodiversity strategy had not yet been finalised or submitted to the CBD Secretariat, and the government was not expected to make any additional financial commitments to support developing countries in implementing the Global Biodiversity Framework. These messages gained a big media coverage in Finland, as WWF Finland’s comments on the meeting were covered in several regional newspapers as well as in national media outlets, such as Helsingin Sanomat and MTV. In total there were over 100 media hits considering the topic. An important lesson on communication was gained by the success of detailed press briefings. As some environmental topics are complex, such as international commitments for climate and biodiversity, it is key to provide information for the media in a clear form, while still taking into account various perspectives. In advocacy work and communications there have been challenges to find new channels to cover for the downfall of X. Many organizations, experts and even policymakers have decided to leave the channel, including WWF Finland. There is still work to do in finding other channels as effective as X used to be in its better days. WWF Finland has provided training for its experts on the topic in early 2025, and as a new channel, Bluesky is now in its testing phase in the WWF Finland communication palette. The programme partners play a key role in showing how global interconnections manifest in different parts of the globe. Partnering countries and the WWF network provide WWF Finland with various communication materials, which are translated and edited to Finnish audiences (examples are given from Madagascar, Mekong area & Congo basin and Tanzania). WWF Finland’s communication expert also participated in a monitoring trip to West Papua in order to gather authentic material. These stories were appreciated by the audience in various channels even if the media space was dominated by big international topics, especially security concerns. Additional human resources provided through the programme in 2024 enabled WWF Finland to continue its advocacy on the interlinkages between climate change, nature loss and conflict – a theme that has gained increasing attention in recent years. Climate change and nature-loss not only threaten human security, resilience and well-being, but also stability on a local, national and global level.

During the Partnership week in Finland the participants got to know WWF Finland’s onground work, including wetland restoration. © SILJA HONKAVUORI / WWF

The international WWF network has identified conflicts and instability, alongside corruption (which is linked to conflicts), as key challenges for successful conservation. To address this issue, the WWF network has formed a Fragile and Conflict States (FCS) Working Group, aimed at raising awareness and strengthening the organisation’s resilience in fragile contexts, with WWF Finland playing an active role in its efforts. It is worth noting that awareness raising is key – in some occasions, conservation activities could also be a catalyst for discontent and thus, instability.

In 2024 it became even more evident that the topic of climate, nature and security is relevant for both WWF’s work on the ground and in advocacy.

In 2024, WWF Finland produced, among other things, communications materials exploring the interlinkages between drought and (in)security (article and Instagram video), published an oped on environmental and climate security before the presidential elections, organised and attended a panel discussion at the Crisis Management NOW event, and held meetings with government officials, NGOs, UN agencies and other organizations on this topic. Also, together with The Finnish Institute for International Affairs, we organized a seminar on the impacts of war on the nature in Ukraine. During the visit of WWF Ukraine’s CEO to Helsinki, meetings were held with Finnish stakeholders engaged in work related to Ukraine. An outlook

WWF FINLAND 2025

to the situation on the ground in Ukraine was given and an opportunity to discuss not only the environment, but the role of NGOs in Ukraine and possible cooperation with Finnish stakeholders. These discussions clearly demonstrated that WWF Ukraine’s priorities align well with those of Finland in Ukraine, revealing numerous opportunities for synergy. WWF Ukraine also has deep knowledge and important contacts that can be relevant and useful to Finnish stakeholders. Finnish media also interviewed WWF Ukraine’s CEO, and the environmental costs of the war were covered in WWF Finland’s own channels. In 2024 it became even more evident that the topic of climate, nature and security is relevant for both WWF’s work on the ground and in advocacy. Training partners and the network on these issues has proven valuable, not only in building capacity, but also in fostering dialogue within Finland and in international negotiations. Partner offices have different levels of understanding of said issues but already many of them acknowledge the role of climate change as a threat multiplier. Meanwhile, the regional Africa Adaptation Hub has surpassed its programme targets, driven by increasing demand for adaptation support and strengthened by strategic partnerships that have enabled deeper engagement with both duty bearers and rights holders.

RESULTS BASED MANAGEMENT

Coffee plants grown in agroforestry in the programme area in Laos. © SAOSAVANH KETMALA / WWF

WWF FINLAND 2025

MONITORING AND EVALUATION AND ADAPTIVE MANAGEMENT WWF Finland monitors the programme via regular (monthly or quarterly) calls with partners, quarterly financial reports, technical reports, active email communication and monitoring visits. Implementing WWF offices monitor programmes locally. Programme progress is tracked through the Results Framework and its indicators, as part of the annual reporting process. Mid-Term Review The mid-term review of the programme was conducted in 2024 by an external evaluator. The findings and recommendations of the review consolidated WWF Finland’s own views on the programme. Some recommendations were too general to take action upon, especially when country specific information was not included in the review report. The recommendations of the review and the observations from the monitoring trip raised the need to work closer with the partners on some themes like business plans and sustainability of the restored areas (survival rate of the seedlings). The partners were given an opportunity to comment on the findings of the mid-term review in a joint session with WWF Finland and the external evaluator. The findings were used to strengthen partnership and cooperation in the years ahead, and served as a foundation for the WWF International Innovation Team’s facilitation efforts to explore innovative ways of setting future goals and identifying pathways to achieve them. WWF Finland will engage its partners in discussions on the sustainability of the supported approaches during the final year of the programme and in preparation for the upcoming programme period.

The programme is on the right path to achieve its outcomes and ultimate impact statement.

WWF FINLAND 2025

The key findings of the mid-term review (MTR) helped consolidate WWF Finland’s own understanding of the programme. The programme is on the right path to achieve its outcomes and ultimate impact statement. The programme design represents a necessary, sufficient, appropriate and well-founded approach to bring about positive change in targeted biodiversity issues. There are no challenges on setting the objectives and targeted impacts and the focus of the programme is relevant. Also, the programme Theory of Change was considered clear, which supported WWF Finland’s decision to continue to use it as a basis

for planning of the programme for 2026-2029. The overall efficiency of the programme in terms of quantity, quality and time is good. The costs of the intervention are justified by the programmelevel achievements. The review team also highlighted feedback from WWF Finland and the Ministry for Foreign Affairs (MFA) regarding the sustainability of the programme’s approaches – an issue WWF Finland will discuss with its partners in 2025. There were recommendations in the MTR related to five topics:
1. Sustainability of reforestation and restoration activities. Capacity building in maintaining the trees, monitoring methods for tree survival rates and consideration if a small fee could be charged for the seedlings to improve the commitment of the farmers in caring for the trees planted.
• These will be discussed with the partners.
2. Livelihoods and private sector development. Availability of technical expertise for livelihoods development, proper business plans and feasibility studies, assessment of stakeholders’ capacities and the companies should be invited to contribute to the activity design when there is potential to involve private sector entities.
• WWF Finland will continue to engage with, and to support partner offices on these issues.
3. Collaboration with governments.
• WWF Finland didn’t fully understand the recommendation to continue the current approach not to exclude any country or region from the programme due to potential challenges in the collaboration with the government. There are no plans to reduce the number of partners and definitely not because of possible challenges with the local government. Changes in governance structures and collaboration agreements should be considered in risk assessments. This will be further discussed with partners when reviewing their risk matrices.
4. WWF Finland added value and cross-programme collaboration. WWF Finland’s added value to its partners could be further increased by making its expertise in many topics accessible to programme partners through active capacity building and sharing of experiences.
• More collaboration opportunities for sharing experiences and learning from programme

partners could be organised. WWF Finland can provide more support on different themes if / when partners express their needs.
5. Programme scope, management, monitoring and evaluation. Considering if the number of partners could be decreased, the expertise of the nature-peacesecurity nexus should be maintained or strengthened at WWF Finland and further development of indicators.
• These recommendations were considered when planning for the next programme phase. Recommended increase in the evaluation budget will be done in the next programme phase.

MONITORING VISITS In 2024, the following monitoring trips were done:
• Uganda. District officials are very positive about the collaboration done under the programme. There are positive indications of organisational development and ownership establishment within the Tree growers and Timber traders co-operative (committees, own time and resources used for further development of the site and organisation). Civic space is constrained in Uganda.
• Kenya, monitoring of East Africa Wildlife Crime Hub activities, capacity building on climate, nature and conflicts and participation in the UNEA meeting as a part of the Finnish delegation. The main observations from the visit were that the Hub is doing very meaningful work, and would require more human resources for communications activities etc. In addition, it was noted that the Hub staff and key stakeholders, including local NGOs and the Kenya Wildlife Service, have good knowledge of the interlinkages of climate change and security, which was demonstrated in Kenya during the historical droughts in 2024.
• First visit to Papua in Indonesia. It was observed that nature in the programme area remains largely untouched, with exceptionally rich biodiversity and cultural values. WWF support in the very remote area is required and highly valued. WWF Papua team has good relationships with many stakeholders, from local communities to government partners. The support to indigenous groups is very important and has specific value. The Embassy of Finland was met in Jakarta. Highquality communications material was collected and produced, thanks to the participation of a communications expert on the trip.
• Madagascar. The programme has started

WWF FINLAND 2025

collaboration with HELVETAS, which is supporting the implementation and capacity building of the communities on the livelihood’s development, especially on vanilla. The collaboration has been delayed for approximately 1,5 years due to a long contracting process. Project sites and communities are very remote and hard to reach. Local communities rely heavily on vanilla cultivation for their livelihoods. To reduce vulnerability to market shocks and the impacts of climate change, livelihood diversification is strongly recommended. Communities are committed to working with WWF and appreciate external recognition. WWF has established working relationships with local officials despite resource constraints. The habitat of the world’s smallest chameleon, endangered Brookesia nana, was also visited during the monitoring visit, and the photographer that accompanied the team produced visual material of the species.
• Laos. Deforestation is at a very high level in the country and WWF prioritises securing the most valuable forest areas, such as the protected areas where WWF Finland support also focuses. With park resources severely limited, WWF’s support remains crucial for strengthening collaboration between the parks and surrounding communities, both to halt deforestation and to promote ecological restoration. Bureaucracy is high and processes for official agreements are delayed. Finally, WWF Laos got a MoU for this project after a 2.5 year delay. In addition, the following trips by WWF Finland staff were carried out under the programme:
• The International Forest Expert visited Brussels in a meeting of European and Brazilian WWF offices around the EU deforestation law and joint actions.
• The International Programme Director attended the COP16 in Cali Columbia as part of the Finnish delegation.
• The Programme Expert attended WWF staff training on UN Human Rights Mechanisms and conservation in Geneva. During the training, WWF staff got the opportunity to meet with UN staff, representatives from other organizations, special rapporteurs and researchers and learn about how human rights and conservation are interlinked, but also how to use human rights mechanisms for conservation impact. The WWF network will publish a toolbox on this topic in 2025. The main observation from the trip was that, while climate change is widely recognised within the UN human rights discourse, biodiversity remains a more complex and less integrated

issue that still demands significant attention. WWF could have a meaningful role in advocating for more attention to biodiversity issues, and WWF Finland would be well-equipped to do this, since we have been closely following human rights issues in the UN due to Finland’s role in the UN Human Rights Council and as human rights have a central role in Finland’s foreign policy.
• The Senior Conservation Officer took part in a WWF Inclusive conservation workshop in the Netherlands on joint Northern European office efforts to advance inclusive conservation.

•

•

In late 2024, WWF Finland also tested the concept of a long monitoring trip, where a WWF Finland expert spent five weeks in Indonesia / Papua to strengthen the equitable partnerships and strategic narrative and vision of conservation work conducted in Papua especially around inclusive conservation, locally led NbS and adaptation. Some general observations and lessons learned were gained from the monitoring trips:
• Monitoring trips enable WWF Finland to better understand the real and actual challenges on the ground. Experience from the trips together with findings of the mid-term review guided WWF Finland to focus discussion with the partners on some of the more challenging themes (business plans and sustainability of restoration work).
• Monitoring trips have enabled WWF Finland to get to know the partners better and form more open relationships. Because the programme was planned during COVID-19 restrictions and for the first couple of years of the implementation traveling was limited, WWF Finland has finally now visited all partner countries. In the future it would be advisable to visit and meet especially the new partners during the first year of the implementation.
• Monitoring trips and joint processes together with partners (especially during the long monitoring trips) are opportunities to strengthen and build more equitable partnerships and enable stronger localisation of the programme approaches. The visits to partner country offices, right holders, duty bearers and other stakeholders can be utilised for more co-creation and implementation rather than inspection of work and achievements.
• As several partner offices were visited in 2024, it was noted that partners may implement the same approaches quite differently, which is understandable due to different working environments in the countries but might also mean

WWF FINLAND 2025

•

•

•

that more quality control is needed. The need is increased by high staff turnover in partner offices. WWF Finland could also include more detailed thematic questions to the monitoring check list and possibly challenge the ways some approaches are implemented. The monitoring trips could be planned more strategically at the beginning of the programme period to serve the programme purposes and to potentially focus some of the trips to one theme or geographic area as required. Monitoring trips are quite extensive and many issues and items need to be covered in often very challenging environments. WWF Finland together with its partner might want to consider that some monitoring trips could have thematic or other scope and the whole project site and all activities would not have to be covered. WWF Finland could also ask from partners what kind of monitoring or thematic dialogue they would like to have with WWF Finland. On practical travel arrangements, it was found to be useful that the monitoring trips are carried out by two experts. This enables better understanding of the partners work and provides our partners broader feedback. It also allows cross-checking of observations. The participation of a communication expert has added value to the monitoring trips and WWF Finland has gained authentic communication materials from the partner countries. WWF Finland international programme experts have also produced social media material from the trips without the help of a communication expert. Some of the programme coordinators are new and may not have experience in arranging monitoring trips. WWF Finland should clarify the objectives of the trips, as well as practical arrangements, such as the amount of down-time etc.

WWF Nepal organized a virtual monitoring visit via Zoom in May 2024. Invitation was also sent to programme coordinators in other programme countries and all WWF Finland staff. Zoom session was not recorded in order to make the event comfortable for local right holders who were speaking. Virtual monitoring visits are a great opportunity to present project interventions to multiple people at the same time and interactively. However, based on the experience of two organised virtual monitoring visits, they cannot replace actual monitoring trips. In virtual meetings there’s no possibility to choose who you want to talk to or where you want to visit, and video call participants see only what the person responsible for streaming in the field site chooses to show. Unofficial chats

An exit strategy was developed and the support to Borneo was phased out by the end of June 2024.

during evenings and car travels can be very valuable, whereas on video time to ask questions is limited. Furthermore, on virtual visits, the sites must be chosen based on the available internet connections and still the connection is usually breaking while sending live video from the field. 2024 was also the last year that programme supported Borneo. An exit strategy was developed and the support to Borneo was phased out by the end of June 2024. Other funding was secured from Finnish Relex – foundation for the Borneo – team to continue working within the landscape. Result framework By the end of the third year of the 4-year programme, most of the outputs and outcome targets have already been achieved. This has raised a question whether the programme target setting has been ambitious enough during programme design and should be further elaborated at the end of the programme. The logic for setting baselines has not been completely consistent among all partners and as a result some baselines have been revised during the programme. For the next programme period the baseline setting will be discussed in more detail with all partners to ensure unified logic. The following changes were made to the baselines and targets of Result Framework in 2024:

Political instability, shifts in government priorities, and changes in public administration personnel are identified as risks in several partner countries.

WWF FINLAND 2025

• Outcome 1 Indicator 2a “Size of areas (hectares) put under environmental or watershed protection”. Baseline is 55 671 ha. Earlier it was 105 671 ha, because there was a mistake and what should have been in target (50 000 ha in Papua), had been accidentally put in the baseline. This has been rectified.
• Outcome 1 Indicator 2b “Size of areas (hectares) put under sustainable forests management”. Baseline is updated from 298 465 ha to 297 782 ha. This is because the baseline in Tanzania was revised from 683 ha to zero.
• Outcome 1 Indicator 2c “Total area (hectares) of forest landscape brought into restoration since 2020”. Target revised from 18 375 ha to 18 515 ha.
• Outcome 2 Indicator 1 “No. of Nature Based Solutions and adaptation projects, policies and / or initiatives adopted”. Baseline updated from 50 to 39, as the target in Nepal was revised; smaller interventions were grouped into 4 more impactful NbS concepts.

RISK MANAGEMENT Each partner office has their own risk management system and keeps their own risk registers; they follow the programme’s risks either in a programme specific risk register or as a part of the office’s risk register. WWF Finland keeps a programme level risk register which has been made using WWF Network’s risk register template. At programme level there are 30 risks identified. Risks are classified as external or internal, and into six categories: People (staff), Strategic & Programmatic, Financial, Operational, Reputation & Fiduciary and Environmental & Social. Risks are discussed with partners during monitoring visits and regular calls, annually as bare minimum. In Finland, risks are discussed in the quarterly programme update meetings and current risks are summarised in the weekly meetings of the WWF Finland’s international programme team. Following a recommendation from KPMG, WWF Finland international programme team established an incidence log to systematically track issues emerging in the programme, and to follow-up their resolution. WWF Network has a Risk Management Hub that provides guidance, material, training and support on risk management to WWF offices. WWF Network’s ESSF and FPIC processes are also part of the risk management portfolio. Political instability, shifts in government priorities, and changes in public administration personnel are identified as risks in several partner countries. These risks are mitigated by establishing strong relationships, maintaining active dialogue and communication with authorities at all levels. It is also important to keep conservation and development on the agenda, together with CSOs and NGOs. 2024 was the hottest year in recorded history and nature loss is unfolding at pace. Climate crisis and loss of biodiversity increase the likelihood of natural disasters and, thus, the importance of preparing for them. These disasters are gaining media attention in Finland. WWF Finland decided to establish a Fund for Natural Disasters which increases WWF Finland’s fund raising capacity and enables quick support to address natural disasters and increase preparedness in Finland and globally. First fund raising event was organised for the severe forest fires that took place in the Amazon region in the latter half of 2024.

The Iténez river in Bolivia. © JULIAN HAHNE

The specific target was WWF Bolivia, which is also a programme partner. A total of EUR 40,000 of extra funds (in addition to programme funds) were raised and channelled to WWF Bolivia for the after-care of the affected areas, as well as to prepare for the next wildfire season. It is again evident that impacts of climate change have had an effect on the programme implementation. The lack of adequate rainfall during the last rain season in Tanzania meant that the planting of trees had to be postponed to 2025. In Laos, the survival rate of the planted trees was low due to the lack of irrigation water. In Madagascar, a cyclone destroyed community tree nurseries and affected 13 CBO villages, which slowed down restoration and community engagement efforts. In Bolivia, forest and wildfires prompted an urgent need for additional support to the affected communities and areas. Support was channeled from programme budget as well as from WWF Finland’s separate fund raising campaign. In order to tackle climate change impacts in Nepal, the programme has implemented mitigating and adaptive measures such as forest management and restoration, bioengineering, disaster risk reduction, and diversifying livelihood options for vulnerable communities. WWF Finland together with the WWF network was closely following the alarming trend of decreasing

WWF FINLAND 2025

ODA funding in 2024. There has been a marked decline in ODA contributions from several European countries central to WWF network funding, compounded by USAID’s cuts in early
2025. These will impact the WWF network but there were no direct impacts reported in those countries and landscapes which this programme is supporting, in 2024. WWF network will continue its advocacy work towards increased climate and biodiversity funding targets set in the Paris Climate Agreement and the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. At the same time the network is building its internal capacity and understanding of fundraising from different sources of finance. In Nepal, injuries and casualties due to wildlife encounters are on the rise and likely to affect local communities’ tolerance for conservation initiatives. WWF Nepal, in collaboration with government agencies and local communities, is implementing both proactive and reactive strategies to foster coexistence. Key efforts include developing Human-Wildlife Coexistence models, enhancing community awareness and preparedness such as securing livestock through improved corrals, strengthening rapid response and compensation mechanisms. EUR 25,000 from unallocated budget was added to Nepal’s budget in 2024 to address HWC.

FINANCIAL MANAGEMENT The workplan and budget were revised four times in 2024. All revisions were sent to and approved by MFA. In 2024, unallocated budget (EUR 137,000 + admin 7 %) was used for several activities. These allocations were included in the budget revisions that were submitted to MFA during the year. The amounts were added to the budget of the applicable partner, and amendments to the agreements were drafted and signed.
• Nepal, HWC (Human Wildlife Conflict) activities including preventive measures (such as early warning system, predator proof corrals, awareness), remedial measures (such as immediate relief and skill/livelihood support for victim families), and rescue of problematic/victim animals. EUR 25,000
• Nepal, for the development of the concept with the Red Cross. EUR 5,000
• Africa Adaptation Hub, to hire a consultant fundraising specialist for up to 6 months to identify funding opportunities for regional initiatives and write funding proposal to mobilise funds for NbS and climate adaptation. EUR 20,000
• Indonesia, Arabela landscape (in Borneo) to finalise activities and processes in 2024, including: 1) to continue cooperation with task forces / forums and networks / partners to advance sustainable and equitable development in landscapes and 2) to continue to strengthen and support right holders’ and duty bearers’ capacity in developing community based sustainable forest management, business practices, supply chain, sustainable land use management and forest restoration. EUR 20,000
• Madagascar, to additional MEL activities, including CSO and CBO evaluation in 2024. EUR 7,000
• Tanzania, to support the mid-term review of Forest Landscape Restoration Africa Initiative. EUR 10,000
• Africa Adaptation Hub, to hire a communications consultant and an assistant for the Hub. EUR 10,000
• Finland, mineral survey. EUR 20,000
• Nepal, for policy advocacy toolkit for integrating NbS for climate adaptation and disaster risk reduction into national adaptation plans (NAPs), nationally determined contributions (NDCs) and the Sendai Framework for disaster risk reduction. EUR 10,000
• Tanzania, for sustaining VLFRs (Village Land Forest Reserves) management. EUR 10,000

WWF FINLAND 2025

EUR 7,700 from Finland’s M&E budget was allocated to Indonesia for the expenses of inclusive conservation workshops in Jayapura and Jakarta in November 2024. Programmes were audited in respective countries, using the template provided by MFA. The costs of WWF Finland, as well as the programme level report, were audited in Finland by PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC). Additional financial audit in Uganda In late 2023 WWF Finland commissioned an additional financial audit to WWF Uganda covering Finland’s support in calendar years 2020-2022. WWF Finland has previously considered this form of additional auditing and decided to initiate it in Uganda, the programme’s largest partner with an annual budget of EUR 350,000–400,000. The exercise included several lessons learned which are separately documented and summarised below:
• Define and confirm the timeline for the audit with the partner office taking into account possible holidays and negotiate if there are changes on the timeline. Make sure that relevant staff in the audited office are available during the time of the audit.
• Clearly specify the scope, number and nature of visits.
• Discuss and agree on the publicity of the audit report in the very beginning of the exercise.
• WWF Finland must submit the report to the primary donor (MFA) and they must submit all correspondence with the development aid receivers upon request to any interested party (Act on the Openness of Government Activities).
• Ensure that the engagement during the audit enables all parties to be updated on the process and understand where possible delays are caused.
• On the procurement of the service:
• We only received one quote. There must be enough time for the procurement process so that the service providers have time to submit a bid. WWF Finland was not able to get recommendations from other Finnish NGOs or network partners. Explore more efficient ways of distributing the request for quotations.
• Direct procurement by WWF Finland may lead to double VAT liabilities; both domestically and in the programme country. A potential mitigation measure could be to explore joint procurement arrangements with the audited WWF Office.
• Local auditors were cost effective and flexible.

Monitoring practises (monitoring check list) were updated in 2024 based on KPMG recommendations and WWF Finland’s own observations.

In general WWF Finland and Uganda agreed that the exercise was useful and WWF Finland will continue conducting similar audits in the future. Based on this audit WWF Finland emphasised the need to include light financial checks to all monitoring visits. There were six actual findings from the additional audit in Uganda. They were related to the supporting documentation for expenditures (format of documents or missing documents), missing policies to guide the payment of travel costs to participants for programme activities, lack of binding agreements or MoUs with the tree grower associations or cooperatives, late submission of reports and late remittance of statutory deductions. Supporting documentation was not found for two items of expenditure (from Oct 2022 and March 2021), totalling UGX 1,563,000 / EUR 374. This amount was reported to MFA and agreed that it will be refunded to WWF Finland. This was done by decreasing the budget of WWF UCO under Resilience programme 2022-2025 by 374 EUR. An amendment to the agreement to this effect was signed in November 2024. KPMG review WWF Finland and the programme was reviewed in early 2024 by KPMG, as mandated by MFA. The review went well and the review report included nine minor risks (corrective actions are to be taken simultaneously with other relevant measures) and one moderate risk (corrective measures are to be carried out within a reasonable time i.e. 6-12 months). WWF Finland implemented most of the actions specified in the management response already in 2024 and MFA approved WWF Finland’s management response and actions during the annual discussion in December 2024. The moderate risk was about the visibility of the WWF Finland’s whistleblower channel which has now better visibility at the WWF Finland website. This channel will be also mentioned in new contracts with partners. Other minor risks considered risk management at WWF Finland and incidence log, monitoring practices, cooperation with the partners and the network, procurements, PSEAH, monitoring practices and procedures for managing possible conflicts of interest, which WWF Finland already noted in 2024, as feasible. The programme has established an incidence log to track issues emerging in the programme and continue regular update

WWF FINLAND 2025

meetings with WWF Finland senior management to ensure up-to-date information sharing of the programme activities and possible risks. Monitoring practises (monitoring check list) were updated in 2024 based on KPMG recommendations and WWF Finland’s own observations. WWF Finland created PSEAH guidance and will discuss with programme partners about PSEAH in 2025. WWF Network has started a process to strengthen its and WWF offices’ individual capacities in PSEAH. WWF Finland will continue the dialogue with the network on how to share information about the country offices and how to better coordinate the support from different country offices.

FINANCIAL SUMMARY The total available budget for the programme in 2024 was EUR 3,802,687, out of which EUR 3,232,284 was MFA support and EUR 570,403 self-financing. The total costs of the programme in 2024 were EUR 3,358,639. The spending was 88 % of the available annual budget. Compared to the original 2024 budget (without the carry-forward amount from 2023), spending was more than 110 %, hence the delayed start of the programme activities in the first year of the programme is still impacting the burn rate. In Africa Adaptation Hub, Laos, Indonesia, Bolivia and Uganda the reported achievements were fully funded by this programme. In Tanzania, this programme’s contribution is 23 % of the Water Towers Landscape but reported activities were fully funded by this programme. In Nepal, for the output level, reported achievements were fully funded by this programme. For overall Terai Arc Landscape (TAL), this programme’s contribution is approximately 21 % and for Western TAL 78 %. In Madagascar, reported achievements were 95 % funded by this programme. Outcome 1 and Outcome 2 were fully funded by this programme; under Outcome 3 there was also funding from Sweden. From the total Northern Highlands Landscape’s funding, this programme’s share was around 17% in 2024. For East Africa Wildlife Crime Hub, this programme covered 28 % of the Hub’s annual budget in 2024. This programme’s contribution to reported activities varied between 30 - 100 %.

Expenses in the least developed countries (Madagascar, Tanzania, Uganda, Laos and Nepal) were EUR 1,513,521, which is 45 % of total expenses. Expenses in the fragile states (Madagascar, Tanzania, Uganda and Laos) were EUR 1,127,494, totaling 34 % of the total. In addition to the Partnership Programme, WWF Finland supports the WWF network offices through a network service fee which was EUR 1,014,269 in FY2024. This funding is used to support the WWF network, including offices in Africa and Asia, e.g. in organisational development and compliance of the network policies. WWF Finland established a Fund for Natural Disasters in 2024. The first fundraising effort supported forest fire relief in Bolivia, to which WWF Finland contributed EUR 40,000 from the Fund, on top of existing programme funding.
